title: Every check here proves it can still fail on each push
description: A passing check can mean a clean tree or a check that stopped reading it. Three checks here read zero files for up to 60 days while every build went green. Plant each one's defect in the browser and see which go blind.
bodyHtml:
Every check here proves it can still fail on each push

Every check in this repo makes two claims: it passes on a good tree, and it fails on the defect it guards. CI tested the first claim on every push. The second was tested once, by hand, in the PR that added the check, and 20 commit bodies record a "Controls:" run that never ran again. In between, three checks read zero files for up to 60 days while every build went green.

A green check is half a measurement

A check that passes says one of two things: the tree is clean, or the check stopped looking. From the outside they read the same. Invariant 8c fails the build when a Garage page has no entry in site-manifest.json. The www/ split in #457 (2026-08-18) left its walk pointed at public/garage, which still held av2/ and lean/ assets but no .html. The directory existed, so the walk succeeded, found nothing, and reported nothing unregistered. It inspected 0 of 39 pages for 60 days.

The only way to tell the two apart is to plant the defect and see whether the check notices. That's a control: the edit that reintroduces the bug, the check that must catch it, and the words the check prints when it does. Since 2026-10-30, tools/lib/controls.ts keeps each one as data, and bun run controls plants every one on every push.

The bench

Four checks from this repo, rebuilt small enough to run in your browser. Each runs twice, the way the harness runs it: once on a good tree, which has to pass, and once with its defect planted. The first box replays the change that blinded the real check. The second applies the fix it got.

Press the first preset. Every good tree still passes, which is all validate could see that week, and every planted defect sails through. Then turn on the walk's drift and its floor together: the good tree goes red. The floor leaves the walk reading the wrong directory and refuses to call the empty walk a pass, so the move that blinds the check fails the build it lands in.

Four verdicts, and why the words matter

The harness reads each planted run as one of four verdicts. CAUGHT: the check went red and printed its own line. BLIND: it passed with the defect in place, which is the finding the harness exists for. WRONG REASON: it went red, but something else failed first. STALE: the text a mutation anchors on has moved, so the defect can't be planted. A contract test in validate fails on STALE, so the PR that refactors a guarded file has to move its control too.

WRONG REASON is why every control quotes its check. The first serendipity control planted its conflict marker as bare code. Bun's parser failed the build before the scan ran, so on the tree before #1390 the harness read WRONG REASON where the truth was BLIND. The marker now sits inside a template literal, where the module still parses and only the scan can see it. Tick "plant it as bare code" on the bench to watch the same thing happen.

Before any control runs, each distinct check runs once on an unplanted clone and has to pass. A check that's already red proves nothing by going red again.

What the first runs found

deploy-command pinsno check read the 4 deploy scripts outside infra.json0 of 4 scriptsalwayswriting a control, #1488

The first three were found by accident. Replayed against the trees before #1390 and #1408, the harness reads BLIND on all three, so it would have caught each one the day it opened. The last three it found itself, within a day of landing. Gotcha 13's walker is the expensive one: it guards the encodeBody flag that a rebuilt Response drops, and for 70 days a rebuilt Response on the noindex path could drop that flag and the walker would pass it.

What it costs

Each control plants into its own copy-on-write clone of the worktree: one clonefile(2) call, about 130 ms on 2026-10-29. Other sessions work in the same tree, so a planted conflict marker must never land where one of them could commit it. In CI the checkout is private, so the runner plants in place and puts every touched file back.

The registry went from 11 controls on 2026-10-30 to 25 the next day and 44 on 2026-11-09, covering 11 gotchas. On 2026-11-09 all 44 read CAUGHT across 28 distinct checks in 94.1 s on a 12-core M3 running four clones at a time. CI ran the 42 then on main in 81.3 s. The job reports beside validate with continue-on-error. A blind check is a finding about the checks, so it never holds up a release.

What it can't see

A control proves a check catches the one defect someone wrote down. A defect nobody planted stays invisible. The deploy-pin gap had no check at all, and the harness found it only because writing that control sent someone looking. Coverage is still a list a person keeps, so gotcha 90 asks every new check to arrive with its control in the same PR, quoting the line the check prints when it catches.

editorial.reader: Someone who maintains a CI pipeline and reads a green check as proof the code is clean.
editorial.problem: A passing check can mean the tree is clean or that the check stopped reading it, and CI shows those two the same way.
editorial.thesis: A check is measured only once it fails on purpose, so this repo plants each check's defect on every push and flags the check that stays green.
evidence: Three checks here read zero files for 1 to 60 days while every build passed; replayed against those trees, the harness reads BLIND on all three.
Writing the next controls found three more blind spots within a day, one of them 70 days old.
The bench runs four of the checks in the browser, before and after the change that blinded them.
editorial.uncertainty: The harness proves each check catches the defect someone planted. A defect nobody wrote down stays invisible, so coverage still depends on a person adding the control.

understanding.intro: Four questions on why a green check is half a measurement.

questions.q: Invariant 8c passed every build for 60 days while it inspected 0 of 39 pages. What would have exposed it on the first day?

options.t: Planting an unregistered page and seeing the build stay green.
options.why: Right. A planted defect that passes is the only signal a blind check gives. The good tree looked the same either way.

options.t: Running the check twice to see whether its output changed between runs.
options.why: A blind check is deterministic. It passes the same way every time, so a second run adds nothing.

options.t: Reading the build log for the check's summary line.
options.why: 8c printed no count before #1390, so its line read the same whether it walked 39 pages or none.

questions.q: The first serendipity control planted its conflict marker as bare code. On the tree before #1390, what did the harness report?

options.t: BLIND, because the scan still matched only files ending in .js.
options.why: That was the truth about the scan, which is the problem. The parser went red first, so the harness never saw the scan pass.

options.t: WRONG REASON, because Bun's parser failed the build before the scan ran.
options.why: Right. The build failed for another reason, so the run proved nothing about the scan. A marker inside a template literal lets the module parse and leaves only the scan able to see it.

options.t: CAUGHT, because the build went red with the marker in place.
options.why: The control expects the scan's own words, and the parser's error doesn't contain them, so red alone proves nothing about the scan.

questions.q: #1390 gave invariant 8c a floor: fail when the walk reads under 30 pages. What does the floor change about the next refactor that moves the pages?

options.t: The check starts finding unregistered pages in the new directory on its own.
options.why: The floor leaves the walk pointed where it was. All it adds is a refusal to call an empty walk a pass.

options.t: The good tree goes red on the next build, so the move can't merge quietly.
options.why: Right. A walk that reads 0 pages now fails on a clean tree, so the refactor that blinds the check is the build that breaks.

options.t: Nothing until someone plants a page, since the floor runs only then.
options.why: The floor runs on every build. A walk under 30 pages fails the clean tree, which is the point.

questions.q: On 2026-10-29 the gotcha 16 guard passed locally on a new file that CI then failed. Why?

options.t: The local Bun ran a different parser version than the one CI installs.
options.why: Both run the pinned Bun. The difference was which files the scan was handed.

options.t: Its scan listed files with git ls-files, which skips unadded files.
options.why: Right. ls-files reads the index, so a file nobody has added is invisible locally and present once committed. 19 of 22 scans had the same blind spot.

options.t: CI plants defects in place, while local runs plant them in a clone.
options.why: That's how the harness runs, and this guard wasn't under the harness yet. The scan itself never saw the file.
